newsitem.title: USA: Religious freedom central to U.S. policy - Albright.
newsitem.headline: Religious freedom central to U.S. policy - Albright.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Thursday that questions of religious freedom were central to U.S. foreign policy.

Addressing a committee on religious freedom abroad, Albright said recent disclosures about Nazi persecution of her Jewish ancestors strengthened her resolve to create "a living monument" to those who suffered for their beliefs.

"The issue of religious freedom belongs squarely in any comprehensive discussions that we should be having and are having about American foreign policy," she told the special advisory committee to the secretary of state.

Albright said she was "very interested" by the number of times she was asked about religious questions during hearings before Congress earlier this week, when she was testifying on the State Department's 1998 budget request.

Freedom of religion was "central to America's history and identity" and was "an original component of America's historic and continuing effort to promote democratic values and respect for human rights", she said.
If State Department officials understood about religious persecution and thought about ways to build tolerance "we all will be much more capable diplomats," she said.

Albright referred to recent media reports -- which she has said came as news to her too -- that three of her grandparents were Jews who died in Nazi death camps in Czechoslovakia, where she was born. Albright was brought up as a Roman Catholic and later became an Episcopalian.
"My childhood understanding of life under a totalitarianist threat has already left me with very firm beliefs about the requirements of a free society, one of which is freedom of religion," she said.

"Those beliefs have not changed. They don't need to change. If anything, I am more eager to work with you and to make our cooperation a living monument to all those who have suffered for their beliefs throughout history and all those who suffer today," she told the committee.
The committee, set up last November and holding its inaugural meeting at the State Department on Thursday, groups prominent American religious figures of different faiths.
U.S. officials said its aims were to study growing religious persecution around the world and examine ways to support efforts of those trying to promote tolerance.
